title: Scientists Demand Billions for Sky Geoengineering to Combat Climate Crisis, Times Reports
body:
A consortium of climate researchers is calling for an unprecedented influx of public and private funding—potentially running into the tens of billions of dollars—to develop and test large‑scale geoengineering techniques that could artificially cool the planet. The proposal, which bundles together a suite of controversial approaches ranging from “cloud brightening” to solar radiation management, is being presented as a last‑ditch complement to emissions cuts, aiming to buy humanity time while the world transitions to net‑zero energy systems.

The most prominent ideas on the table involve deliberately altering the Earth’s reflectivity. One method, marine cloud brightening, would spray fine seawater droplets into low‑lying marine clouds, making them more reflective and sending a fraction of incoming sunlight back into space. Another, stratospheric aerosol injection, would disperse sulphur‑based particles high in the atmosphere to mimic the cooling effect of volcanic eruptions. Proponents argue that these techniques could be deployed relatively quickly and at a fraction of the cost of full‑scale decarbonisation of industry and transport.

Skeptics, however, warn that the scientific, ethical, and geopolitical ramifications are far from settled. “We do not fully understand the side‑effects of tinkering with the climate system on a planetary scale,” said Dr. Lina Patel, an atmospheric physicist at the University of Cambridge. Potential risks include disruptions to regional precipitation patterns, unintended acceleration of ocean acidification, and the creation of a “moral hazard” where governments might postpone essential mitigation measures, assuming a technological fix will appear later. Moreover, the governance of any deployment would require unprecedented international cooperation, as unilateral actions could have cross‑border consequences and spark diplomatic tensions.

Funding the research is another contentious point. The consortium’s budget estimate runs from $30 billion to $50 billion over the next two decades, a sum that rivals the annual investment in renewable energy subsidies in many developed economies. Advocates argue that the cost is justified when measured against the projected economic damages of unchecked warming—estimated in the trillions of dollars by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). They also point to the potential for commercial spin‑offs, such as advanced aerosol delivery systems, that could offset some of the public expense.

Policy makers are now faced with a delicate balancing act. On one side, there is mounting pressure from climate activists and vulnerable nations to explore every possible avenue to curb temperature rise. On the other, legislators must grapple with the prospect of allocating massive resources to technologies that remain largely unproven and could trigger irreversible side effects. Several governments have already signaled interest in pilot projects; the United Arab Emirates, for instance, announced a $1 billion grant for a cloud‑brightening field trial, while the European Union is debating a dedicated research fund within its Horizon Europe framework.

If the scientific community can demonstrate, through transparent and rigorously peer‑reviewed experiments, that these geoengineering tools are both effective and safe, they may become a critical component of a multi‑pronged climate strategy. Yet the path forward will require robust international legal frameworks, clear accountability mechanisms, and a steadfast commitment to continue aggressive emissions reductions. As the planet edges closer to the thresholds that could trigger irreversible climate feedbacks, the debate over whether to “engineer the sky” is likely to intensify, shaping the next chapter of global climate policy.
